extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on composing the lead and body of a news story, including types of leads, organization, accuracy, tone, and presentation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Present facts with judicial impartiality; avoid warping the narrative by unfair arrangement or a prejudiced point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not willfully suppress information or distort news; unbiased stories (or as nearly unbiased as possible) are required. Legitimately ordering topics for effect (humor, pathos, etc.) is allowed, but never let desire for effect distort facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult City Editor before Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before beginning a story, report briefly to the city editor and ask for instructions about handling and any features to play up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the editor an account in as few words as possible; be ready to produce copy quickly. Be prepared with two or three alternative leads when the editor's preference is unpredictable. If no instructions are given, proceed but file copy promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize Two Kinds of Leads
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is the first sentence or group of sentences; there are two principal types: the summarizing lead and the informal (suspense) lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summarizing lead gives the gist concisely and is far more common and recommended for beginners. The informal lead introduces the reader without revealing outcome and is used to create interest when the news itself is weak or commonplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarizing Lead — form and length
rubrics_metrics.description: The summarizing lead may be a single sentence, a paragraph, or several paragraphs depending on complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short stories usually have short leads; long, involved stories may use a multi-paragraph summarizing lead and sometimes display the summary in black-face type before divisions with individual leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of the Lead (Who, What, When, Where, Why, How)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should feature what will be of greatest interest to general readers and begin with the most important fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the lead answers the questions who, what, when, where, why, and how; play up the primary feature of the story (result, cause, name, place, method, time) depending on reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: Put Most Important Facts First
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the lead, put the most important fact(s) at the very beginning rather than time, place, or weak modifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid beginning with 'to-day', 'to-morrow', 'yesterday' or with weak articles unless necessary. Feature result and cause/motive, or the method, name, place, or time as appropriate to the story's most newsworthy element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of the Lead — grammatical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of grammatical form depends on purpose; common types include simple statements, series, conditional clauses, substantive clauses, infinitive phrases, participial phrases, prepositional phrases, and absolute constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the form that best emphasizes the important detail; be mindful of clarity and modifier attachment (especially with participial phrases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads with Short Sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Using short sentences (one or a few) in the lead grants forcefulness and emphasis to individual important details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break a long summarizing lead into a very short sentence followed by longer ones, or into several brief sentences each giving an important detail to increase impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional-Clause Lead (use sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads beginning with conditional clauses are valuable for humorous effects or summarizing but can become heavy or obscure if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using more than two conditional clauses in a lead to prevent sentences from becoming unwieldy or obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive-Clause Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with a substantive clause enables direct or indirect questions and allows important ideas that normally come at the end to be moved forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to begin with a reported statement or testimony that sets up the story; ensure grammatical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase-Based Leads (Infinitive/Participial/Prepositional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads beginning with infinitive, participial, or prepositional phrases can bring out emphatic details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care that participial phrases have definite nouns to modify to avoid dangling modifiers and ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute-Construction Lead (advanced; avoid for beginners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute constructions can forcefully feature causes and motives but tend to be un-English and make sentences unwieldy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using absolute constructions if inexperienced; reserve for writers comfortable with complex syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and Interest in the Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads must possess both accuracy (truthfulness) and interest (to lure readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material so the lead presents facts that are both true and likely to interest readers; interest should not be achieved at the expense of accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness — avoid overloaded leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads must be clear and not crowded with details that blur the initial sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lead is overloaded with details, cut it into two or more short, crisp sentences. If the reader cannot grasp the lead readily, they likely won't read on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boxed Summaries for Long or Complex Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story is unusually long or complicated, prepare a digest of principal items and box them in display type before the regular lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boxed summaries are typically decided by the city editor, but reporters should suggest groupings. Common candidates: accidents (lists of dead/injured), sporting events (records/crowds/gate), speeches/trials/executions (key utterances), diplomatic letters, lengthy reports. If unsure, prepare a boxed summary on separate paper for the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal (Suspense/Human-Interest) Lead — purpose and difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal leads begin with a question, verse, startling quote, or minor details to whet reader appetite and are used for news that is old, commonplace, or distant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They require originality of approach and statement; because they demand creating attractiveness out of weak news, they are more difficult and should be attempted after mastering summarizing leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question Lead (type of informal lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with a question can entice readers when the answer frames the discussion or precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for engaging readers' curiosity, but ensure the follow-up provides useful context or precedents so the question is meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse Lead (type of informal lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting with a bit of verse can attract attention but is difficult due to uncertainty in metrical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly; ensure meter and relevance are competent enough not to distract or diminish the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-Statement Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an extraordinary quotation or statement from a speech/interview/trial can serve as an informal lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the quoted statement effectively summarizes the story it becomes a summarizing lead; otherwise use it to entice, ensuring accuracy and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense Lead (type of informal lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begins with seemingly unimportant but enticing details and lures the reader paragraph by paragraph toward the main point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most difficult informal lead; it must sustain half-promises and avoid losing the reader by promising too little or making the payoff unsatisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone — lead should suggest story tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should suggest the tone of the story (pathetic, tragic, humorous, satirical, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a lead that imbues the intended tone; success in suggesting tone correlates with the story's overall effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's Recommendation: Start with Summarizing Leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Novices are advised to attempt only the summarizing lead at first because it is definite and can be checked against the who/what/when/where/why/how test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the news itself to carry the story; practice informal leads later when your hand is sure, as informal leads require achieving elusive effects like climax and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body Composition: Maintain Interest and Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: After a strong lead, the body usually follows as a simple chronological narration with interspersions of explanation or description; the reporter must maintain the interest and accuracy developed by the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize details wisely so the following parts 'tell themselves'; guard against the two chief crimes: inaccuracy and dullness, with inaccuracy being the greater offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in the Body — avoid imagination and rash conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must avoid inventing details or jumping to conclusions to make a story more interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inaccurate reporting harms the paper's reputation, can lead to legal judgments, and injures innocent persons; provide verified facts and resist the temptation to embellish or speculate without evidence.
